records.sourceFile: Early tendon morphology as a biomarker of long-term patient outcomes after surgical repair of Achilles tendon rupture - A prospective cohort study.pdf

paper.citation: Saarensilta A, Aufwerber S, Grävare Silbernagel K, Ackermann P. Early Tendon Morphology as a Biomarker of Long-term Patient Outcomes After Surgical Repair of Achilles Tendon Rupture: A Prospective Cohort Study. The Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine. 2023;11(11):23259671231205326.
paper.abstract: Achilles tendon rupture outcomes vary and are hard to predict. In 86 adults who had surgical repair, ultrasound tendon cross-sectional area and elongation were measured at 6 weeks, 6 months and 12 months. A larger CSA ratio at 6 weeks was associated with better heel-rise height symmetry at 12 months, and greater elongation at 12 months was associated with poorer total concentric work symmetry.
paper.tldr: In surgically repaired Achilles ruptures, a larger tendon cross-sectional area on ultrasound at 6 weeks was linked to better heel-rise height symmetry at 12 months. Greater tendon elongation at 12 months was linked to poorer work symmetry. These are single-cohort associations, not validated clinical tools.
paper.methods: Prospective cohort study using data from a randomized trial of early functional mobilization versus cast immobilization after acute Achilles tendon repair (2013 to 2018). Ultrasound measured CSA and tendon length at 6 weeks, 6 months and 12 months, with 12-month outcomes from the Achilles tendon Total Rupture Score, heel-rise endurance test limb symmetry indices, and multiple linear regression adjusted for age with AUC analysis.
paper.findings: The 6-week CSA ratio was associated with LSI maximum heel-rise height at 12 months (n = 45, adjusted R2 0.35, P < .001; AUC 0.82 for LSI above 80%). Greater TE at 12 months was associated with lower LSI total concentric work measured at the same visit (n = 82, adjusted R2 0.21, P = .001; AUC 0.71, which the authors call diagnostic rather than predictive). CSA ratio at 6 months with ATRS, TE at 6 months with LSI total concentric work, and TE at 12 months with LSI heel-rise height were not significant after Bonferroni correction (threshold P < .0019).
paper.limitations: Postoperative regimens differed between the trial groups, rehabilitation was not standardized after 6 weeks, only three time points were measured, and not all patients were measured at every time point. Only surgically treated patients were included, the predictive values were not externally validated, and the 12-month elongation finding is concurrent with the outcome, so its predictive value is unclear. The participants' athletic status is not described.
paper.practicalImplications: Ultrasound tendon measures may be worth tracking in research on Achilles rupture recovery, but this study does not show they should set rehabilitation or return-to-sport decisions. Clinicians should not treat the 6-week CSA ratio as a validated prognostic tool based on this cohort alone.
paper.athleteDev: The study does not measure athletes or sport performance, so it cannot inform training prescription. Its heel-rise and work outcomes are functional measures after rupture repair, and any use for athletes would be an inference beyond this data.
paper.rtp: The study does not test return-to-sport criteria. It found that a larger 6-week CSA ratio and greater 12-month elongation were associated with heel-rise and work symmetry at 12 months, which may guide research but should not be used alone to clear or delay return to sport.

records.sourceFile: Eccentric training decreases paratendon capillary blood     flow and preserves paratendon oxygen saturation in chronic achilles     tendinopathy.pdf

paper.citation: Knobloch K, Kraemer R, Jagodzinski M, Zeichen J, Meller R, Vogt PM. Eccentric Training Decreases Paratendon Capillary Blood Flow and Preserves Paratendon Oxygen Saturation in Chronic Achilles Tendinopathy. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2007;37(5):269-276.
paper.abstract: Twenty adults with chronic Achilles tendinopathy were randomized to 12 weeks of daily eccentric training (n = 15) or a control group (n = 5). Laser Doppler and spectroscopy measured paratendon microcirculation at 8 sites and 2 depths. Pain fell 48% in the eccentric group, and some superficial capillary flow measures decreased, while oxygen saturation was preserved.
paper.tldr: In this small randomized trial, daily eccentric training reduced pain by 48% in chronic Achilles tendinopathy. Some paratendon blood flow readings fell within the training group, but the between-group flow difference was not significant. Oxygen saturation was preserved.
paper.methods: Randomized controlled trial with 15 patients in eccentric training (3 sets of 15 repetitions daily for at least 12 weeks) and 5 controls who used cryotherapy and relative rest. Laser Doppler and spectroscopy (Oxygen-to-See) measured capillary blood flow, tissue oxygen saturation, postcapillary venous filling pressure and blood flow velocity at 8 paratendon locations and 2 depths before and after 12 weeks. Pain was rated on a 0 to 10 visual analogue scale.
paper.findings: Within the eccentric group, pain fell from 4.1 to 2.1 on the VAS (48%, P < .05); in controls it fell from 8.0 to 5.5 (P = .123). Superficial (2 mm) capillary blood flow fell within the eccentric group at the medial distal midportion (-31%, P = .008) and lateral proximal midportion (-45%, P = .016 in the abstract and .04 in the results text), while controls showed similar or larger nonsignificant median drops at several sites, and there was no significant between-group difference in blood flow. Tissue oxygen saturation did not change in either group, and superficial postcapillary venous filling pressure rose within the eccentric group at the medial and lateral insertion sites.
paper.limitations: The sample was small, with 5 controls, and the control group had higher baseline pain (not statistically significant, P = .086). The abstract reports a deep midportion blood flow decrease and reduced deep filling pressures, and the discussion reports a between-group flow difference, but the results and tables show only superficial within-group flow decreases, superficial filling-pressure increases at the insertions, and no between-group flow difference; the two text sections also give different P values for the lateral site. Laser Doppler outputs are uncalibrated arbitrary units, adherence to the home program was not verified, and the many within-group tests were not corrected for multiple comparisons.
paper.practicalImplications: Pain fell within the group doing daily eccentric training for chronic Achilles tendinopathy, but pain was not formally compared with the small control group, and the trial does not show that eccentric training changes tendon blood flow relative to control. Clinicians should not use paratendon microcirculation measures to judge treatment response based on this study.
paper.athleteDev: The study measured pain and tendon microcirculation in recreationally active patients with tendinopathy, not athletic performance or training adaptation. It does not support a performance claim.
paper.rtp: The study does not test return-to-sport criteria or tendon load tolerance for sport. Its pain and microcirculation results cannot be used to judge readiness to return to sport.

records.sourceFile: Effectiveness of conservative interventions after acute hamstrings injuries in athletes - A living systematic review.pdf

paper.citation: Afonso J, Olivares-Jabalera J, Fernandes RJ, Clemente FM, Rocha-Rodrigues S, Claudino JG, et al. Effectiveness of Conservative Interventions After Acute Hamstrings Injuries in Athletes: A Living Systematic Review. Sports Medicine. 2023.
paper.abstract: Living systematic review of 14 studies (730 athletes) comparing conservative treatments for acute hamstring injury on time to return to sport or full training and reinjury. No intervention was superior for any outcome, and the only signal was limited, very low-certainty evidence that eccentric lengthening shortens time to full training. Platelet-rich plasma did not consistently shorten time or reduce reinjury.
paper.tldr: For acute hamstring injuries, no exercise-based rehabilitation approach was shown to be better than another for return to sport or reinjury. PRP did not reliably speed recovery or reduce reinjury, and the eccentric lengthening signal is preliminary.
paper.methods: Searches of seven databases to January 2022, plus manual searches, citation tracking and expert consultation; PRISMA 2020 and Cochrane methods. Risk of bias was judged with RoB 2 and ROBINS-I, exercise-program reporting with i-CONTENT, and certainty with GRADE. Results were synthesized narratively because the studies were too few and too heterogeneous to pool.
paper.findings: Fourteen studies with 730 athletes were included; most were judged at high risk of bias, and only three had low risk of ineffectiveness for their exercise programs. Eccentric lengthening (L-protocol) was followed by a shorter time to full training than the C-protocol in two trials (28 vs 51 days; 49 vs 86 days), but these trials had selection and detection problems. PRP gave mixed results against placebo or no injection, with a faster time to full training in some trials, no difference in others and no consistent effect on reinjury; low-level laser therapy showed no difference in return to sport versus placebo.
paper.limitations: Few studies per comparison, high risk of bias, and very low GRADE certainty for all outcomes; no pooled estimates were calculated. Several reinjury percentages in the text do not match the Table 2 counts (for example 0.8% and 3.6% for the C-protocol versus 1/38 (2.6%) and 2/28 (7.1%), and 6.7% and 8.0% for Hamilton et al. versus 2/26 (7.7%) and 3/28 (10.7%)), so the Table 2 counts should be used. Competitive level was unreported in three studies and sex was unreported for four participants.
paper.practicalImplications: On this evidence no exercise-based rehabilitation approach should be prioritised for reducing reinjury risk, so protocol choice should rest on other factors. Eccentric lengthening was the only exercise approach with a signal for earlier full training, and it is worth testing as a hypothesis rather than a standard. PRP should not be expected to shorten return to training or reduce reinjury, and LLLT added no clinical benefit to exercise in the one trial that tested it.
paper.athleteDev: This review gives performance staff no basis to choose one hamstring rehabilitation protocol over another for reinjury prevention. The one signal, eccentric lengthening for faster full training, comes from two trials from one group and is very low certainty.
paper.rtp: This review is directly about time to return to sport and full training after acute hamstring injury, but it supports no specific protocol for return to sport. It does not support PRP or LLLT as accelerators, and it cannot set return-to-play criteria because the included studies used inconsistent criteria.

records.sourceFile: Exercise progression to incrementally load the Achilles tendon.pdf

paper.citation: Baxter JR, Corrigan P, Hullfish TJ, O'Rourke P, Grävare Silbernagel K. Exercise Progression to Incrementally Load the Achilles Tendon. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2020.
paper.abstract: Laboratory study of Achilles tendon loading across a battery of rehabilitation exercises, walking and running in healthy adults. The authors combine peak load, loading impulse and loading rate into a loading index and use it to propose an exercise progression that increases tendon loading in steps, with separate sequences for isolated ankle and multi-joint movements.
paper.tldr: Achilles tendon load was measured across rehabilitation exercises in eight healthy adults and ranked into four tiers. Single-leg hopping produced the highest loads (up to 7.3 bodyweights), so the ranking may help order loading, but it has not been tested in patients.
paper.methods: Eight healthy adults (6 male, 2 female) completed a battery of heel raises, squats, lunges, step ups and downs, jumps, hops and drop jumps, plus walking and running. Motion capture (100 Hz) and force plate (1,000 Hz) data were processed in an open-source musculoskeletal model. Tendon load was estimated as the plantar flexion moment divided by a 5 cm moment arm, and the authors combined peak load (50%), impulse (30%) and loading rate (20%) into a loading index.
paper.findings: Loading index values rose from seated heel raises (0.100 for two-leg, 0.128 for one-leg) to single-leg hops (0.904 to 0.924). Walking scored 0.359 and running 0.600. Single-leg heel raises and two-leg drop jumps had similar indices (0.493 vs 0.519) but different peak loads (3.0 vs 3.6 bodyweights) and loading rates. For lunges, the trailing leg had a higher index than the leading leg (0.435 vs 0.285), mainly through longer time under load.
paper.limitations: The study used eight healthy, recreationally active adults and did not measure patients, so the loads are not patient data. Tendon load was estimated from joint moments with a constant 5 cm moment arm, and the scaling weights were chosen from the authors' clinical experience, which they say could be debated. The Results text gives the seated heel raise indices the other way round (single-leg 0.100, double-leg 0.128) from Table 1 (two-leg 0.100, one-leg 0.128); Table 1 values are reported here. The Discussion refers to 25 exercises, while Table 1 has 30 rows that also count walking, running and leading and trailing legs separately.
paper.practicalImplications: Use the tiers as a reference for ordering loads, for example moving from seated heel raises (Tier 1) toward single-leg hops (Tier 4). Single-leg heel raises and two-leg drop jumps have similar index values but different peak loads and loading rates, so they should not be treated as interchangeable. The authors suggest walking and running as milestones for adding exercises with similar index values, and lunges and step ups can be used to load one side more than the other.
paper.athleteDev: Relevant to staff who reintroduce jumping and hopping, since single-leg hops produced the highest measured Achilles loads (peak 7.3 bodyweights). It reports tendon loading values for these movements, not performance outcomes.
paper.rtp: Can inform the staged loading of the Achilles tendon during rehabilitation, with walking and running suggested as milestones. It does not show that any exercise or tier is safe for return to sport, and because the sample was healthy adults, the loads cannot be used directly to judge tendon tolerance after rupture or tendinopathy.
